title: Chinese Tomato Egg Soup: The 10-Minute High-Protein Comfort Meal
excerpt: With just tomatoes, eggs, and a few pantry staples, this classic Chinese comfort soup delivers warmth, nutrition, and Indo-Chinese nostalgia in minutes flat.
body:
Few dishes bridge the gap between "I have no energy to cook" and "I need something genuinely nourishing" as cleanly as Chinese tomato egg soup. Known in Mandarin as xīhóngshì jīdàn tāng, this home-style soup requires little more than ripe tomatoes, a couple of eggs, broth, and 10 minutes. The result is a bowl of silky egg ribbons floating in a tangy, umami-rich tomato broth — the kind of meal that feels restorative without demanding real effort.

A Chinese Classic With Indo-Chinese Soul

Tomato egg soup belongs to the canon of Chinese home cooking, a category of dishes so elemental they rarely appear on restaurant menus in China. Ripe tomatoes are sautéed until they break down, then simmered in chicken or vegetable broth. Beaten eggs are poured in a thin stream into the rolling broth, forming delicate ribbons — or "egg flowers," as the Chinese name more poetically describes them. A cornstarch slurry gives the soup its characteristic glossy, slightly thickened body.

For Indians, the dish carries a second layer of familiarity. Tomato egg drop soup has been a fixture on Indo-Chinese menus across India for decades, served alongside hot and sour soup and crispy noodle starters. Chef Sanjeev Kapoor features his own version, using egg whites, tomato ketchup, and white vinegar — hallmarks of the Indo-Chinese adaptation that Indian diners grew up with.

Nutritional Profile: Light but Substantial

According to nutritional data compiled by SnapCalorie using USDA databases, a standard serving contains approximately 130–162 calories, with 10–13 grams of protein, 6 grams of fat, and 13 grams of carbohydrates. The protein comes primarily from the eggs, which supply all nine essential amino acids along with choline, vitamin B12, and vitamin D. The tomatoes contribute vitamin C, dietary fiber, and lycopene — an antioxidant linked to cardiovascular health.

"Beaten eggs are poured in a thin stream into the rolling broth, forming delicate ribbons — or "egg flowers," as the Chinese name more poetically describes them."

The calorie count shifts depending on broth base and cornstarch quantity, but the soup stays firmly in "light meal" territory. Australian-Indian food blogger Sneh Roy of Cook Republic offers an Indo-Chinese take with vegetable stock, ginger, garlic, tamari, and white vinegar, clocking in at 119 calories per serving.

The Recipe: Five Steps, One Pot

You will need two to three ripe tomatoes (about 400 grams), two to three eggs, four cups of broth, two tablespoons of cornstarch mixed with water, a tablespoon of light soy sauce, a teaspoon of sesame oil, and spring onions for garnish.

Heat a tablespoon of neutral oil in a pot. Sauté chopped tomatoes for three to four minutes until they soften. Pour in the broth and bring to a simmer. Stir in soy sauce and sesame oil, then add the cornstarch slurry and cook for another minute until the soup thickens. With the broth at a gentle simmer, pour beaten eggs in a thin stream while stirring in one direction to create silky ribbons. Turn off the heat immediately, garnish with spring onions, and serve.

"When you salt a tomato, it starts the process of osmosis that draws out the inner concentrated tomato liquid through the cell membranes. It makes the tomato less watery and more concentrated in flavour."

— Sneh Roy, Cook Republic

Adapting It Abroad

For Indians overseas, the ingredients are available at any standard grocery store — no Asian market trip required. To push the soup toward the Indo-Chinese profile familiar from restaurants back home, add minced garlic and grated ginger to the sauté step, swap soy sauce for tamari, and finish with a tablespoon of white vinegar for that sharp, tangy edge. A pinch of white pepper and chopped fresh coriander complete the transformation.

For extra protein, add cubed silken tofu. Drop in spinach or mushrooms for more substance. The soup reheats reasonably well, though the egg ribbons lose some delicacy — best eaten fresh from the pot.
